newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Yilmaz faces severe economic problems.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Yilmaz faces severe economic problems.

text.p: New Turkish Prime Minister Mesut Yilmaz will be faced with pressure to act quickly in tackling the country's severe economic problems.
Economists say the fragile state of the economy, beleaguered by chronic inflation and big public deficits, will be undermined further without rapid measures.
"The government should take urgent measures to solve structural problems, worsened by the previous government and months of political turmoil," a government economist said.
The economy achieved a mainly consumption-driven growth of 7.9 percent last year, but economists say Turkey should attain a sustainable inflation at moderate rates instead of sharp ups and downs.
The foreign trade deficit soared to $19.3 billion last year from $14.1 billion in 1995. The current account showed a deficit of $4.4 billion last year after $2.3 billion a year earlier.
Despite promises by former governments for single-digit inflation, Turkey has been struggling with chronic inflation for the past two decades.
Year-on-year consumer price inflation was at 77.5 percent at the end of last month and businessmen expect it to stand at around 80 percent at the end of this year.
The public deficit, a major reason for high inflation, was around nine percent of the country's gross domestic product.

The former government of Necmettin Erbakan, which aimed at a zero budget deficit, has not announced any budget figure so far this year. But economists expect the deficit to be around 500 trillion lira in the first five months of this year.

State Minister Gunes Taner, expected to be responsible for the treasury and privatisation in the new government, said the the balanced budget target was unrealistic and a supplementary budget would soon be needed.

Government officials say new finance minister Zekeriya Temizel, a former senior ministry official in charge of state revenues, is expected to focus on measures to widen the tax base and prevent leakage.
According to the protocol signed by the three coalition parties, the government will lower tax rates to widen the tax base.
To eliminate fiscal imbalances, the government should also curb public spending, farm subsidies and losses of social security institutions and state economic enterprises, economists say.
The 11-year-old privatisation programme has so far raised only some $3.2 billion which economists say is too low compared to the size of the economy.

State Minister Taner, a leading advocate of the free market and lessening the role of the state in the economy, is likely to push through privatisation. However some MPs from the left-wing partner of the three-party coalition, the Democratic Left Party has blocked several privatisation laws in the past.
"All problems will be overcome with a fine tuning within the free market economy," Taner told reporters.
He also said the government might replace senior economy officials, many of them appointed by the former Islamist-led government.
Government sources say former treasury deputy undersecretary Mahfi Egilmez, now working for a private company, is expected to replace present treasury head Mehmet Kaytaz.
Privatisation chief Ismail Karakaya and general managers of leading state banks are also likely to be replaced, they say.
